Now a longer more explicit review consisting of cons, pros and tips.

Cons: 
-Low playercount resulting in
-> Long queue times. 
-> Bad matchmaking (partially as only veterans stay to play)

-A lot of important mechanics to learn 

Pros: 
-The music. This game has awesome tracks and a unique one for each character! Even if you are not interested in the game you may want to check out the songs.

-Unique gameplay. While having characters with abilities is nothing new. I personally do not know any games similar to omega strikers (if you know any good ones tell me!!!). 

-Interesting characters and lore. While the lore has little to do with the game itself it is still nice to have. And the character design is well executed. Everyone is memorable in its own way. 

-The emoticons. There is no ingame chat during a match (a voicechat has been added but i have never seen it used.) Instead there are plenty of emoticons which can be used. The worst insult there is in this game, is someone spamming thumbs or questionmarks to someone else, who messed up. But usually the players are nice and i love these stickers! They also include a lot of memes. 

-The community. While not everyone enjoys joining a community or social interaction with randoms on the internet. The community is nice. 


Gameplay Tips for new players: 
As a veteran myself and having a friend who totally didnt get forced to play this game with me i got some tips. 

-Strike, the basic "ability" everyone has. Play around your opponents and pass to teammates. 
Use walls as the core bounces of them and do not play the core into the enemies hands. If you cannot pass a teammate, you usually want to keep the core away from your goal or far away from enemy players. 
Additionally often times it turns into a game of "chicken". First to hit the core loses as the strike has a short but significant cooldown.

-Dodge/Burst. Probably one of the more complex mechanics there is. Even after 170 hours of gameplay i still forget about dodging at times. 
What is it? On keyboard by default placed on "Q" is an option every striker has.
It needs energy to be used and charges by collecting green orbs or by hitting the core and enemies. As the name says you can use it to dodge. If you are about to get knocked out the map or about to take a massive hit (and notice it in time) use it to dodge any incoming ability for a little while. Do not use any abilities while dodging as this will cancel the dodge and make you vulnerable again. Collecting enough energy replaces the dodge with burst. This shoves enemies away and makes both you and the core unhittable for anyone but yourself + you hit the core a lot harder/faster this is incredibly powerful.

-Abilities. Practise makes perfect. It may take some time to learn but at some point you will get to know each character and what they can do. If there is one you hate or like in particular read the description and/or try out the abilities in a practise mode or in a match.

-Awakenings. Last but not least the items. During the game you get to choose items to improve certain stats or abilities of your character. Just like abilities it is something one has to learn and sort of memorise. They also come with a handy description so you do not need to know all by heart. Just know what you need, which depends on your character and how you want to play.

It's not an uncommon sentiment that jumping into Ranked ASAP results in a better experience for new players more often than not.

In spite of this, this game truly is something special that I believe a lot of people can enjoy if they can get their feet in past these initial hurdles. I truly wish to see it succeed- if not now, in the future.

And beyond all that, it's free! At the very least, I'd say it's well worth giving it a shot.

Positives
1. The emotes in this game were the best emotes I have seen in any other game.
2. The characters are all very well designed, in-game interactions via dialogue is great, and concepts are well executed. Really makes you want to check out and play new characters.
3. Base gameplay is really fun. Dodging opponent skillshots while trying to get core control is very addicting. Lots of room for strategy, skill expression, and satisfying set up plays. It is very fast paced, and it is possible for all positions to "carry" the team to victory.
4. The way you get items in this game is nice, allows for midgame strategy and comeback setups, I think it was a great implementation so far, but I do wonder if it can get snowbally in higher level gameplay where scaling characters can get choked out.
5. Striker abilities and cooldowns create a low skill floor and a high skill ceiling, making the game very deep if you start learning some mechanics.
6. You can try all characters in the practice mode (this is really nice)
7. There are themes for all characters and if you get MVP your theme plays for next set

Negatives
1. High skill ceiling with stagnant/loyal player pool creates steep learning curve for newer players because they will have trouble finding the buffer of players of similar skill level to them. I think this is exacerbated by the lack of tutorial found inside the game created, not sure how many community created tutorials there were either. (**positive note**: the character trailers showed cool mechanics I could use and broke them down well and are great references)
2. Fast paced, competitive gameplay amplifies a feel of helplessness (especially in goalie position), leading to frustration and toxicity. This is something I feel very similar to fighting games like Tekken, where you can be losing one round after another and it's hard to get your mental back under control. Unlike Tekken though, Omega Strikers has 2 other teammates to blame, and there are certain emotes you can definitely use to BM
3. Lack of a fleshed out practice mode. I think many people look at Omega Strikers initially as a 'casual' kind of game. But because it's such a fast paced PvP, things get very sweaty and you get BM'ed on and then you discover that there is no practice mode? Thankfully when I actually joined there was a rudimentary practice mode, but I think Omega Strikers really needed a practice mode at launch with how deep the game was.
4. Not many cosmetics, and on top of that you don't really feel the need to buy them because they just look alright, and there were no cosmetics for my characters. It didn't feel like the devs didn't want skins in the game, it felt more like the devs did not know which characters to make skins for, and what kinds of skins to make, and when to make skins (manpower/planning issue?)
5. UI feels very... not good? E.g.) I press 'Escape' to customize my profile, but there is a separate button if I want to customize my strikers, and I have to specifically go to the store to unlock strikers? I still don't really know what my rank is until I get placed in a match, I don't know how to report/block toxic people I encounter, etc.

Suggestions
1. Have a more in depth practice mode (Let you place core where you want, make enemy AI do repeated actions)
2. MMR based rank system that takes in casual match performance into rough account, instead of everyone starting from rookie
3. Let users be in practice mode while queuing up for a match (queue times can get long, this is a deep game, let us practice and keep our hands warm)
4. Replay system with adjustable speed
5. Setting to mute emotes/expressions - you can implement text chat too, since it can be muted
6. Feature to block/report users, or make the feature accessible and clear
7. Have a alternative skin (even if it's a recolor) with character release for purchase.
8. Encourage/Incentivize full party play somehow (this game feels like night and day with random players vs. a full communicating squad)
9. Highlight community made tutorials and new player onboarding efforts in-game (UI to access community tutorials maybe?)

Ultimately I think the main problem lay in how people approached the game initially (casual/fast) and ended up getting burnt by how difficult it could be and how helpless the skill gap makes them feel. Then they start giving up and thinking it's not something they want to commit hours getting good at as they get teabagged on and get spammed the 'FREE' emote. No tutorials and a lackluster practice mode are a big problem in Tekken as well, but Tekken is not a team game, offers a story mode, and also does not market itself as a casual, chill game. I wonder if it's the open beta that threw devs off and made people think a practice mode wasn't necessary for full release, but I remember I was really thrown off when I tried to play in May that there was no single player mode anywhere so I could try to troubleshoot my technical issues. Then there was Co-op vs. AI instead of custom/practice mode?

Have you ever wanted to play a game of soccer / aero-hockey 3 on 3 with a selection of inhumanly skilled individuals where quick reaction combines with geometry and strategy all while you attempt to avoid being struck into oblivion? If that’s so, apart of having to tell you have some weirdly specific wishes, then you are going to love this one.

This game might not “strike” you on the first try, but once you get accustomed to it you start to see the wonders it offers. It’s selection of characters it’s one of the most colorful and diverse in current times: From a sentient construct of multiple slime blobs from space to a hamster that was canonically fed so much it anthropomorphized, or even a trio of corporate workers using shady technology to a simple girl whose sheer passion for the sport burns brighter than any flame; all their designs and personalities give life to it. The gameplay on the surface might seem like the usual “just score to win” but that’s merely the first of multiple layers, which include a combat system that gives the option to just yeet the enemy defense away, an equipment system that buffs individual specialties while rewarding good performances with being the ones to pick items first & everyone’s favorite high school subject… GEOMETRY, no really, the amount of points that end up being scored while not aiming directly at the goal is astonishing, all thanks to the slight inclinations around the map (everything according to plan, by the way). On a smaller scale, the maps at the moment tend to technically be the same, just with altered gimmicks like small black holes, water cannons, portals, etc; but every now and then some great mix-ups come out, like the tea time flavor maps which experimented with the goal by moving it vertically or mirrored, although those have been temporary, the chance of them entering rotation is always present.

The only negative I have seen so far is the matchmaking (as many other reviews have noted) with the game itself being a bit rough on newcomers as well. We are talking of a ratio about 2 (Normal) to 3 (Quickplay) matches out of every 5 you play, tend to have 1 player on either team whose performance might drag the team down. This aspect is significantly reduced only on Competitive matches but still present as a possible risk to player rankings. However, this problem isn’t ignored by the devs and it continues to be worked upon it (for real, it was almost League of Legends level of matchmaking on the starting days and has only gone up from there).

Omega Strikers has single-handedly reminded me how fun some online team multiplayer games can be with its fresh concept, colorful cast and caring developers. Every single second I have played and will keep playing is worth it every single time.

Odyssey Interactive has been amazing with their player – developer communications, even in the most recent announcement of a halt of new content next year due to the decrease in players, they still irradiate optimism in expanding this amazing world they have created and I as many others are all here for it. This game is just the start of an ever-growing potential, and I can’t wait to see what the future holds for us.

I love this game, and it’s really fun to play, but as an intermediate player, I can understand why people have a problem with this game having no ELO system implemented. 

It’s REALLY hard for new players to get their bearings in this game. Not only does the tutorial do a pretty poor job getting new players settled, but a new player’s first real game against other players will most likely be matched with pro level players who know all the techniques and such, then get absolutely destroyed by them.
And when the new player performs badly, their teammates, who are likely also experienced players, will start getting upset with them. 

I even tried to get friends to play the game, and they, of course, don’t know jack about the game going in. I would be the only player doing decently, and my friends, understandably wouldn’t perform well. Then we’d be faced with super sweaty players, and my friends would get upset, not just from losing, but from the toxic emote spamming of the enemy players.

That new player experience is a real turn off. 
If we were able to be matched with players of similar skill level, it would help more players to get further invested into the game. 

I do want this game to succeed, because I find it to be a splendid game and fun to play. But if your experience is just playing game after game, losing to skilled players and going against those same players every game after that to lose again and again, who would want to stay for that? 

I really hope the devs see these reviews and take that into consideration. 

Now with that said, I will not recommend this game for new players going in blind as of right now. But if you’re up to the challenge, go right ahead.

i think people should give this game a shot, since its free, but i wouldn't openly recommend anyone to play it for a lot of reasons.

first and foremost, the community is small and seems mostly populated with veteran and tryhard players. even the casual gamemodes feel extremely competitive. it will take a good 20 to 40 hours of game practice just to last longer than a few minutes against even an average team of players.

another thing that makes the game extremely overwhelming is just the sheer amount of things to keep track of. not only is there 3, sometimes 4 separate progressions to chip away at, but even in the middle of rounds theres dozens of characters and items which do keep the gameplay varied, but due to the competitiveness, you better learn about all of them really quick, and be prepared to bring up all of that knowledge even for a short quick play match. it really is a hard game to just turn on and play for a few hours.

the live service plague is also all over this game. luckily all gameplay-focused content is 100% free. big props for that. however the cosmetics are a really big chunk of the identity and personality of this game, so missing out on it is gonna feel disappointing, and not doing that is as much of a grind as one could expect. it compounds with the issue of the game being hard to hop on, meaning play sessions usually have to be focused and multiple hours long to feel exciting and worthwhile.

last and most glaringly is a clear lack of content and polish. im used to avoiding games like these that seem to just release as early, buggy messes devoid of options, so it's a bit of a shock to the system. the gameplay modes are very lacking. the practice mode forces you into the same character, and there is no test mode to try out new characters, letalone for free. the only way to try out new characters is to go straight into the frying pan. the only info you have on how new characters work is a bit of text. many of the characters have zero skins. a majority of the stuff you can buy seems to just be beta-turned-premium content. and you churn through what little the game has to offer with one of the most horrible and broken UIs i have ever had the displeasure of exploring. it is a barely-serviceable mess.

those are the most objective complaints i have. besides that, the only things i find subjectively dissatisfying is that most of the characters are extremely reliant on done-to-death tropes, with their multi-paragraph backstories being describable in one or two sentences to get the picture. the game also HEAVILY, HEAVILY relies on memes for humor. this will either be a huge plus or a source of exhaustion depending on your preferences. it's kinda worn out its welcome for me, and i only have roughly 60 hours on the game.

despite everything ive said here, the game is still getting regular updates, and it really does cost nothing to check it out. maybe we can stick around and pray for things to get better, just like every other live service title. for now, though... yikes.

This is a great game. Honestly a sleeper. If you're a fan of MOBAs or Rocket League or like anything cute semi-anime (it's fully voiced over in Japanese and even has an anime opening with Japanese vocals made by Studio Trigger), then this is the game for you. 

Queue times are usually pretty quick, even on Competitive. There's a character for everyone and I like how every match is different with the rotating item selection allowing for a slightly different game every time. The counterpicking meta as well allows for some strategy when playing Normal or Competitive. 

New content and patches roll out frequently. I LOVE their careful approach to patching. The devs are pretty fun but most importantly they take patching the game very seriously.  It's refreshing to see slow and steady attempt at nerfs and buffs to carefully tune the game instead of a character that's slightly overtuned getting nerfed to obsolescence. The great thing is that every character is viable in their own right. You've got some characters that poke, some that rush, some that are midrangey, and everything in between. They're all unique in playstyle and in aesthetic. 

Also of note, there is no voice chat or text chat, so you can't get called out by your rando teammates for scoring on your own goal or passing to the enemies. You can even hide your own name and stay anonymous if you want that. 

That said, it's DEFINITELY the game you wanna play with two other friends in VC so you can coordinate things. The sheer adrenaline rush of scoring goals is beautiful. Make sure you play your position seriously (i.e. forwards need to keep good positioning and pressure, goalies needs to keep good positioning and reach the core). When you queue with random people, you can set what position you want to cue as so players can be filled in respectively. 

This game is great for both unwinding with games of Quick Play or Normal and for getting so sweaty you need a shower in Competitive. Great game with whoever "the boys" are in your life. You can hop into Quick Play for some super quick matches or hit the Comp grind for a few hours. 

The music is pretty good as well. A lot of the music is actually produced by independent music creators who lend their talent to this game. Every character's theme plays after you are the MVP of a set, and lasts throughout the next set. Each character's theme is unique to that character and gives a great sense of identity to who you play as. 

There's a lot of optional but great looking skins and customizable options for your Strikers. 5 emotes, a skin, and a goal explosion, giving you completely optional freedom to make your striker set up feel unique. 

Overall, 10/10 instant recommend to anyone. Great, well-balanced gameplay, great aesthetic, and most importantly, a passionate development team. Shoutouts to Odyssey Interactive for making a great game and being great devs.

The learning curve. 

This game is incredibly unfriendly to new players, as the game has many un-intuitive designs (e.g. hitting last), confusing descriptions (e.g. what the heck is 600 range), and poorly explained key mechanics (e.g. awakenings). Not only that, the game has been releasing characters and maps that are increasingly more complex, which further makes the new player experience frustrating. Consequently, this leads to many potential newer players leaving the game, which leads to smaller playerbase, which leads to poor matchmaking to those not playing during peak hours, which leads to even smaller playerbase. Odyssey clearly understands this, as they have "recently" released a tutorial, but it is missing so many details that it might as well be barebones. 

I love this game, and have played enough hours to show that, but I just cannot recommend this game to other players.

Please don't let the recent complaints about matchmaking deter you, Omega Strikers is easily one of my favorite games right now and for good reason. Essentially, take MOBA play style akin to League of Legends (which the members of Odyssey worked on), and throw it into an air hockey rink. Although MOBAs are typically slow, OS is a high-speed rush that's super satisfying to learn and master. You won't get it right away, but when it clicks you can pull of some really cool stuff, and it never gets old.

I particularly love the characters, from their intricate designs, to their lore and voice work. Every character has plenty of voice lines that let their personalities shine, such as Drek'ar's stoic tone even as he experiences this new "fun" thing, and X's booming voice that's loaded with energy. On top of this, each character has their own unique playstyle that can be fun to learn. If you prefer playing at a range, there's Estelle who has long projectiles to keep up pressure or stop opposing pressure from ever starting. If you prefer beating people up, there's Juliette, who can focus down key team members and take them out. New characters are being added consistently, the latest of which at the time of writing being Kazan, who wields an umbrella and can flip between ability sets when the umbrella is open or closed.

On the mention of matchmaking earlier, yes, it is in a weak state at the moment. I won't deny that I'm frustrated with it too. But I encourage you to weather the storm with me; Odyssey is a talented team that knows to listen to its community. I'm sure improvements will be made soon. They're very open with interaction with the community, and even do so in unique ways, such as status updates (all the way down to micropatches) being presented by their very own VTuber who also interacts with the community. Legend has it that if you find her in one of your games, you may receive a special emote...

I encourage you to try Omega Strikers if you're looking for a new type of PVP game. It's an experience like nothing else out there right now, and if you put in some time, it will certainly be worth your while.

When in reality its mostly due to a weird tug of war between items and character changes as items are rotated in and out. Similar to league of legends patches, except the person making up the stats here is just rolling a die cause its "fun." 

   Also devs get off to making high ranks not fun by adding restrictions to who you can play with. So instead of splitting between solo and premade queues, they just straight up enforce solo only. CM basically crusades once a week about how bad communication is for the game lol.

  Anyways, overall if you're just in for casual fun with friends and don't plan to climb, game is good. good game, terrible matchmaking ; I'm in mid-gold, and my comp spread ranges from beginner to high platinum, which results in some impossible to win (and lose) games due to the high skill floor and ceiling. If you can through the torturous beginner solo queue experience and get decent at the game, it feels very rewarding to pull off combos, scoring flashy goals, and KOing, especially when your opponents are similar in skill level.

However, the issue with this game is exactly that: while established "good" players can enjoy the game with each other, the new players are not retaining due to the lack of guidance, tutorial, and terrible ranked experience overall (I lost 10 games in a row in ranked when in bronze and that almost made me quit the game). The lack of popularity also means that there's limited resources on guides and improving at specific characters, which means you have to figure out a lot of things on your own. The only reason I stayed is because my friends are playing with me and I have a strong desire to get better and learn the game. Most other people won't have a reason to go through the suffering. If they are not having fun, they would quit this game and play 20 other games that brings them more joy and less frustration. I love the game, but I also understand that others may not due to reasons I mentioned above. Nevertheless, it is a problem that can be fixed with simply having way more players so people won't get matched against others who are two full ranks above them.

If you are new to OS and wonder if this game is worth it, I would recommend you to give it a try and keep a positive attitude; just know that you are going to suck, and you are going to lose, and that's okay. Because when you eventually do pull off that insane play to win the game, that joy is priceless, and the work you put in just made it that much more satisfying.

I want to recommend this game so much, it's so unique, so fun. It's got great music, art looks clean and the gameplay is extremely tight and polished. Lack of optional game modes aside, it's generally a good time.

But there's a severe problem that has been affecting a portion of the playerbase that just seems to get swept under the rug by both the playerbase and the devs, and that's rubber banding.
It's obviously something to do with packet loss and the games inability to handle it, but if affected your character will just run in place and reset to the position the Omega Strikers server last received. This can just be shy of a second, or it can last several.

For some people, they might only get it once or twice a match, while others (like myself) it's a consistent problem that happens several times a minute every single match. For a game that's fast paced, based on reactions and being able to move around in response to (and predicting) a quick object, it's honestly a complete deal breaker. Especially when the only content actually available is mostly just ranked as there's a complete lack of matchmaking outside of it.

The worst of all is the general community reaction to this problem, and the lack of devs acceptance of it. The community either seem to leave, live with it or mostly just sweep it under the rug and pretend it doesn't exist whenever it's brought up. Those that do will often accuse the player of having poor internet. Let me say just now, my internet isn't bad, I have spent a good deal of time fault finding and trying to make sure everything cannot be down to me.
I've tested my internet connection pretty harshly, far harsher than this game will ever stress it. I've made sure that my computer is cleaned up, drivers and device fully updated with no background processes potentially causing issues. Even made sure that it's not other devices causing a problem, taking everything off except my PC. Turning down graphics just in case, trying out different servers.

Nothing fixes this issue. I shouldn't have to be fault finding this, I should be able to pick up a game and have it just work. This isn't my job to do it, but the developers. It's only this game that I have issues with, and it's honestly draining all fun out of what is meant to be an enjoyable experience.
Last night (and today) the rubber banding got so bad that I went from wanting to spend money on the game to outright uninstalling.

For the devs, this problem isn't even on their known problem page. It's not a new problem, this is something that has been complained about for months, if not longer. 
I've heard rumblings from the few people who do seem to acknowledge this problem that the developers are apparently looking to servers so that this isn't an issue. That's great and all, but i'm playing right now. 
If that's genuinely true, please make an article on your website detailing such, provide users with advice on how they can try to fix it in the meantime. At least some readily available communication that this problem has been acknowledged and that it's being taken seriously.

Maybe one day I can come back to this once this problem has been fixed, update my review and change it to an easy thumbs up. But until this issue that's making the game actually unplayable and I cannot recommend anyone pick this up until that's been resolved. 
Sure, it might not happen to you, and that's great if it doesn't. But the problem does exist and it can kill the experience.

Played in the EU region, so some of what I say may differ from other experiences.

I'd like to give praise where it's due at the very least, the game is a unique take on the moba genre in what can only be described as "online air hockey" and the music produced for this game can be wonderful to listen to. It's a fun enough game to try for free if you have nothing better to do, bring some friends and you can co-ordinate some interesting plays and interactions. Surface level, it works.

However, a lot of my grievances from my time playing can only be described as a catastrophic skill issue. The tutorial is bare bones and doesn't actually simulate how to play your character correctly outside of "press A to use skill 1," etc. Bot matches aren't much helpful either, they are definitely more A than I, so the only way left to improve is to try your luck against other players.

Good luck with that - quick play is perhaps a very unbalanced mess of MMR you can hope for, where you're either fighting somebody who just launched for the first time, somebody who climbed all the ranked matches to diamond or whatever grand-master equivalent you can think of, or you get to face those same players but they're using smurf account #3 so they don't have to face as many ranked players themselves - unaware that it is unavoidable at this point. (Region is very subjective coming to this, I've been informed this is mostly an EU player base issue, as most other MOBA type games also suffer from this from my experience as well.) 

Matches are often decided in 5 minutes because of these discrepancies, which may seem fair enough because that's quickplay. However, don't think that ranked is much better, the round format of "best of three," in my opinion, encourages drop outs mid match when getting stomped, having a bad day, or you already know you're going to lose, so what's a timeout or punishment on top of that going to stop you from feeling any worse? I found the fact that relics  you obtain, which can entirely make or break a character, being awarded based on "mvp of the round" to be incredibly annoying and make you feel like you're not improving at times, if you're aware you're constantly towards the end of being picked, you're going to feel worse overall. In addition to this, I've had matches become hostage situations, where the enemy team can be so toxic, that they would rather farm kills on people less skilled at the game, or even stop themselves from scoring goals against you for no good reason other than malice, I assume.

This game had no other form of communication other than emotes and about 4 pre-set commands when i played, I'm aware steps have been taken to remedy this, but the only other way to communicate was by joining the discord. I think this is counter productive to taking online toxicity overall, emote spam is far more irritating than being called a dog online, not being able to communicate real time with voice makes setups outside of pre-made groups very risky, and now you get to be pinged on discord by players of your match about terrible you are. Or maybe they'll say GG at the end if they're not having a bad day and you've faced them twenty times in the last week.

I'd say for a bunch of ex-riot employees that have worked on League before I assume, there is a lot of stuff here I'd say they should've been more aware of from the start in regards to community management. The support team is great though, they changed my named to include the word "scrub" (because that is much more terrible than fighting against people calling themselves "X's feet" or an ad nauseam of it, I guess.) So no complaints there.

I'm aware most of this review is mostly talking about social aspects of the game, but the community surrounding this game can drag it down a lot. I would've never dared actually playing this game by myself without teaming up with friends, and towards the end I gave up actually playing it and just watching people mess around with sound mods I made for it instead.

I didn't care about individual characters in this game, I never got to the point where I would hate an individual character because of their kit or the current meta. Also because to me it was mostly generic anime design and plot in my head, so the story I can't comment about either, but I know it's there. However, certain stage designs are much more notorious then others. There is a lot of randomness to this game when loading into a match that I believe you are expected to adjust around, but I'd rather just pick a character's kit I think looks interesting to play with at the time.

I'd say for a game that was not made for me, I'm impressed I stuck around as much as I did.

To conclude, if you're willing to put up and learn a new set of skills for an interesting take on the moba genre, at least give it a look over, or search up the OST on youtube. Don't entirely base first opinions on my average interactions in game or what I've been told while playing it. This is coming from somebody who hasn't properly touched it in months, but I wanted to leave an updated review because I'm petty and that people are at least slightly aware of what my personal experience with the game was like.

As much as I love the company and the game. As much as I love the community behind this game, the queue kills it.
If you live outside the EU or got two friends that got a strong will to stay at your side even if the game spits at you a bunch of hours in a row. - You might enjoy the game as much as many others do.

But here is a simple fact:
With 365hours played & a year in beta, I can easily sum up how many "fun" matches I had in this game. - Maybe 40.
Majority of the other matches felt like dancing on sharpened lego stones, thanks to the worst matchmaking/queue I've ever seen in a competitive game.

You queue solo:
You will be placed next to two beginners (worst case one or two mobile players) - Your enemy? fully premade team of 3. The dance begins, they pass to each other, no plan to score, just to kill "for fun". - You can't quit. If you do, you get a penalty. The game is designed to be a 3v3, so.. fighting back? no chance. 
*Matches take about 10 to 30 Minutes, depending on how hard you fight back and how fast your enemy wants to finish the match.

If you queue with a full team:
You will be placed against a team of randoms, 1-2 mobile players, maybe one experienced player. - All.. the.. time.
It is as boring as it sounds.

Now for the teamplay:
The game doesn't reward you for playing together.
The more you touch the core, the better your overall rating.
It is important because, after each set, you get to pick an awakening to boost your Striker. Better cooldowns, longer range, multiple skill use. - It's a random pool of 8 items, the better you performed in this match, the sooner you get to pick.
So why would you pass to your team and let them pick before you? exactly.

conclusion:
As amazing the setting is, the music for each striker, the details in the maps, the details in the events and emotes.
It all doesn't matter if the core of the game sucks. Including the beta, we're in the 3rd Season & it hasn't been improved one bit. - I'm starting to lose hope that we ever get a fun matchmaking that makes the game more than a quick one-match-per-day-game.

Omega Strikers is a very fun game. With plenty of characters to choose from, a good variety of arenas, and very good music. However there are some flaws that occasionally rear their head in from time to time, but first the good:

Positives: 

- Lots of characters to choose from, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.

- Pretty graphics with bright and bold colors that make everything really pop out.

- Fast, frantic gameplay with a little bit of strategy mixed in with power-ups and gear.

- Lots of customization options, from skins to emotes to profile icons and much more.

- Great music, every track is a bop to listen to.

Flaws:

- Competitive mode is very unbalanced, mainly due to no similar rank matchmaking leading to one sided curbstomps or vice versa, no stage hazards are disabled, the selection of maps isn't limited, and the 1 character ban feature, the only change comp mode has from normal, often doesn't make an impact if a character no one plays is banned.

- Some characters are clearly stronger than others. Finii, Luna, and Octavia are especially strong.

- Being very team orientated means one missing or afk player can end up killing an entire match for 
that team.

- Odyssey Points are practically never given to you, making some Odyssey Point only content from the store such as Skins, Goal Explosions, and the premium version of the striker passes impossible to get without paying real money. 

- A little nitpicky but could use some Quality-of-Life features such as map filters, an option to disable emotes incase players get annoyed by them getting spammed, and more tactical callouts (I.E. "Defend the goal!", or "I'll play Forward!", etc).

Overall, I think that Omega Strikers is a decent 6 to 7 out of 10 game. The graphics, gameplay, characters are fantastic but the Not-So-Competitive Mode, and the slow power creep of strong characters make the game frustrating when these problems arise. I'd say play it every now and then, and take breaks when needed. Playing too much can leave you frustrated and angry.

Omega Strikers is a fun game with a *terrible* new player experience. Once you leave the tutorial, and you figured you battled enough AI opponents to try a real match, your only real option is going head-first into ranked. That's because every other mode has no skill-based matchmaking. You'll be playing games with much more experienced players who take the game very seriously - and they'll be as frustrated with you, as you are intimidated and out-skilled by everyone else. 

Here's an example: after watching a new player guide, I heard Quickplay was good for when you're new to the game. So I queued in, hoping to play and have fun with some other beginners, only to be put alongside and against players who seemingly had dozens of hours of experience. These were players who I absolutely had no business being grouped with. One teammate got so frustrated with me that, after I finally managed to save a goal, they immediately froze the ball and own-goaled just to end the match. As toxic as that was, it's ultimately the game that put me in there. 

Newcomers and veterans alike get the short end of the stick because you can't play any mode you want and expect to be matched with players of roughly skill. This goes for every game mode outside of ranked, even the more casual ones. If you want to play any of the more casual or for-fun modes, you'll ironically end up in a more serious and less fun match, since you'll be utterly worthless through most of it. And once you do get good enough to take on those modes with confidence, suddenly you'll be on the other side, where you're paired with newbies shaking in their boots, barely managing to hit the ball at all.

So, that means your only option for a fair game is ranked. There's genuinely no place to practice with similarly-skilled players outside of ranked. Which means, ironically, you wouldn't go to unranked to practice for ranked - instead, you'd go to ranked to train for unranked. The only completely stress-free mode is Co-op vs AI, which has been nothing but wholesome (given there's literally no stakes). However, you can only do so many AI matches against the same three AI opponents before things get very boring. 

It's completely backwards, and I have a strong feeling that many new players bounce off of this game because the early experience is so imbalanced unless you stick to ranked or AI battles. No matter how good a game is, if it can't onboard new players, they won't stay for long. Other competitive games, even those this game is loosely compared to - like League of Legends and Rocket League - have that figured out. It's why new players can boot up Rocket League, play an online casual match, and still have some fun. 

Now imagine that same player joined their first match, and found out all five other players were flipping through the air, dribbling the ball flawlessly, passing back and forth with perfect accuracy. And then those same players get annoyed because you missed save a literally dribbled across the ceiling between two players, at light speed, when you haven't even learned to fly yet. That's most of the Omega Strikers experience. It's a terrible experience for everyone involved, unless you're playing with two friends who really couldn't care less.

So, if you really want to get into this game, and actually have a chance to learn the game and enjoy yourself - stick to ranked. You can still practice in Co-op vs AI, but I'd recommend avoiding Quickplay and Normal like the plague. This game can actually be pretty fun, but its unranked matchmaking needs a complete rework.

---{ Summary }---
I've never seen anything like this game. Air hockey x MOBA, Soccer x violence, Rocket League of Legends, there are many names this game could be referred to as, and each one properly represents the incredible incredability of the gameplay. You constantly have to be paying attention to the entire map and be ready to react quickly for the entire game with no slow lulls at all. Fast paced gameplay, huge learning curve, all around awesome fun. Very recommend.

Also the devs are the greatest people ever and true memers.

---{ Graphics }---
The game itself is played in a top-down view, because MOBA, which does limit how attractive the visuals can actually be, but what little they can do, they do in fact do. As far as character design, each character looks great, and each skin is unique and beautifully designed.

Oh, and giant tofu loving hampster.

---{ Gameplay }---
As I said in the summary, the game is extremely intense, especially when you aren't very good at it, like I am. There are two roles you can play. Forward and Goalie. Goalie is a goalie, though most people don't seem to know that (iykyk). A forward can be a variation of things, NOT INCLUDING A GOALIE (iykyk). There are a bunch of different forwards to fit how you want to play. Maybe you want to be more supportive, you could play Era. Maybe you want to be a child with swords who plays much more offensively, try Zentaro.

I've never played a game like this, definitely worth at least trying if you enjoy competitive games.

---{ Audio }---
The voice acting is great, the soundtrack is an absolute vibe, with each character having a theme of their own. Definitely not a game I play muted.

---{ Can you run it? }---
As far as hardware goes, the game is pretty well optimized and should run well on about everything. But... as far as connection speed... Granted, my internet speed isn't the greatest, (3.8mbps down 2.8mbps up as of this review), but I usually get around 100ms alongside occasional packet loss spikes that get a bit annoying. For the majority who live in a place that can get better internet, this won't be a problem, but just be warned.


(My Specs: 
GPU: Quadro RTX 4000
CPU: I7-9750H
RAM: 64GBs)

---{ Will I rage quit? }---
It can get a little bit annoying at times, especially when a teammate doesn't know how to play their role, but I've definitely played more agitating games.

And it's hard to be mad when after a goal everyone starts spamming meme emotes and having some kind of celebratory stroke.

---{ Must I grind? }---
Only if you choose to. You could definitely just play for fun, the only grinding things are account level (cosmetic) battle pass (cosmetic) character affinity (cosmetic) and competitive rank (bragging rights)

---{ Will the story replace my life? }---
Each of the characters has a backstory and there is a pretty good amount of lore, but most of it is just background stuff you have to go out of your way to find out about, and it's pretty much all just to tell you a bit about the characters.

Well-written, but not very important.

---{ Will I have a wallet after getting this? }---
The only things worth buying are skins and the battle pass. You can unlock characters pretty easily, no more difficult than other games with a similar system of having characters to help you play the way you want, such as Valorant.

---{ How buggy is it?}---
There's the occasional problem with little gameplay mechanics, but the devs being the chads they are always get around to fixing problems quickly.

Eh it's alright for a couple hours.

Stale joke aside, this game became my 5th most played on steam for a reason : It's free, it has a cool concept (MOBA meets hockey with some super smash bros added to the mix) and it is my first and only competitive game where I've reached a very high rank (low challenger equivalent to top 1% of the playerbase).

=======================================================================

The good : 

-Very fun character variety, none of the characters feel similar and they each have a unique playstyle. You can be a bully that beats up people with his fists knocking people around like sandbags, a slime girl that can create blobbos that make some sick core (puck) passes to each other before shooting, a space lizard that can camoflage before ambushing unsuspecting preys with his shotgun, a little war crime gremlin girl that can bring a freaking nuke down on her opponents and many more.

-Very simple game mechanics wise, you have 3 abilities to master and that's it. 90% of the combos players will do is either pressing left click (hitting the core) and an ability button or chaining 2 abilities. Due to the fast pace of the game, doing a big combo with the normal left click and all 3 of your abilities is very impractical and would only be a way to flex on your opponents.

-The game puts a bigger emphasis on strategy and prediction over reaction speed. If you're a washed up boomer like me that can't do 0.0001 second flick headshots in your average shooter game or instant flashy ADHD combo kills in MOBA games then you're in luck. The way the core works is that whoever hits it LAST will win the engagement. There is an actual incentive to wait and be patient and let your opponent hit first so you can redirect it elsewhere. Positioning is key to winning games and if you check the discussions tab, you will see a lot of threads going "FORWARDS SPREAD OUT DON'T STAY ON TOP OF YOUR GOALIE". Your common sense (or your lack of it) will determine the outcome of the game more than being a fast clicker.

=======================================================================

The (potentially depending on the player) bad :

-The game is fast paced and can get pretty hectic as the match goes on. Each round has a timer and once it reaches 0, overtime makes the core faster and faster with each hit until it goes so quickly that not even the best players can react to sudden changes in direction. Abilities will fly all over the map, the core will bounce on every single corner possible and you might have no clue what the hell just happened sometimes. Of course, it's part of the fun but a new player might feel overwhelmed by the quick thinking the game requires.

-Non existent matchmaking in casual gamemodes means that if you're a newbie, you have a very high risk to run into high ELO players like me (that are sometimes in a partial or full team premade). They will absolutely stomp your entire team and make you look very silly. This can make your experience extremely frustrating as you'll feel helpless fighting against players that trained for much longer than you.

-Tied to the previous point, this game has a criminally low player count despite being so good. This is in part due to the poor advertising (very little outside of content creators) but also caused by the terrible matchmaking that makes new players slowly lose interest from the game after being stomped repeatedly by high ELO players. This in turn makes newbies even more likely to run into high ELO players instead of people with similar skill level and makes a deadly loop of bad experiences.

-This probably won't concern the average reader of this review, but the higher the ELO, the more the game devolves into what I'd call "Team Deathmatch". In high ELO, there is a very stale meta of abusing characters that are very good at KOing and just killing the entire team before scoring. The devs of this game have sometimes tried to keep them from dominating the meta too much but no matter how hard they get nerfed, they are still a cheap cope out if you want to reach higher ranks easier.

=======================================================================

But all in all, this game is definitly worth checking out, especially since it's free and doesn't take too much space. Who knows, maybe you might end up addicted to it like me !

I want to start off by saying I really, really so bad wanted to like this game. But as it stands now, I just can't, and here's why.

I'll start off on a positive note: I really like the character designs, the personalities they have, the voice acting and the art. The game is so well designed visually it could honestly pass as a triple-A title. It's got some great music, some very amazing character presentations and some ever-expanding lore about the characters and teams.

And while all that is amazing in itself, this game really falls apart when it comes to gameplay and balance.

You see, Omega Strikers was created by Ex-Riot games developers. And if you don't recognize that red flag already, You may remember a very popular game called League of Legends that exploded in popularity many years ago that was created by Riot Games. And while Omega Strikers doesn't play anything like League of Legends, it does incorporate many of League's gaming philosophies and balance structures into it.

And that's bad. That's VERY BAD.

League of Legends is a notoriously unbalanced game and its devs prided themselves on pushing out and silencing the game's casual players in order to appease the competitive ones. Omega Strikers does the same. Deep down this game looks fun and casual but it doesn't want to be a casual game that's fun, it wants to be competitive, it doesn't want you to have fun, it wants to be as competitive as possible.

When you make a game that is trying desperately to have a competitive image for itself you get a mess of unbalanced, broken gameplay that causes absolutely nothing but frustration, especially when you are on the losing team. This usually comes in the forms of Awakenings and Strikers, but sometimes the maps are just as bad as well. 

To add insult to injury, a lot of the awakenings and maps you play on are completely randomized at the start of the match and are completely out of your control. This wouldn't be so bad if awakenings didn't completely and utterly break some Strikers. All it takes is 1 awakening on the right Striker and then it's over, That one player will usually be one hit KOing you and completely dominating the match. For the most part, the strikers themselves are ALRIGHT in terms of balance, Some could use some tweaking but alone they are okay. Awakenings are the issue and honestly, Omega Strikers would be a much, much healthier game if awakenings were just removed. But that's never going to happen. The game is more focused and balanced around Awakenings than actual strikers, there's no way they could ever get rid of them now.

The other issue is monetization. 

This game utilizes the cancerous battle pass system. A monetization system that is heavily criticized for being predatory and manipulative. and though it is a little better than having loot boxes I admit, I still can't help but roll my eyes and groan every time I see a game use battle passes.

To be fair. Omega Strikers also have a shop that you can directly buy from, This includes skins, strikers, emotes and more and I do see SOME things from previous season battle passes eventually end up in the shop, but it would be nice to just let us buy what we want.

My final issue with this game is the "Rotation" system. "Every now and then certain awakenings and maps will be removed from the game and new ones will be brought in, old ones that were removed can be rotated back in randomly at any time. This. is. So. Stupid.

I cannot tell you how stupid this is. It's clear Omega Striokers wants you to be competitive and master your striker of choice but because maps and awakenings are being constantly swapped and rotated out, you simply can't do that. This game will force you to pick strikers based on current awakenings that are chosen and in rotation rather than the striker you want to play. Omega Strikers is desperately forcing a competitive atmosphere on you but then they implement this anti-competitive system that just completely takes all your master of a striker and throws it away. It's incredibly stupid and conflicts directly with what the Devs are pushing Omega Strikers to be, yet it's left in for whatever reason.

In conclusion: This game visually is stunning, the characters are likeable, the game is colourful, the music is amazing, and the presentation is solid.

But gameplay and balance-wise wise it's a total and utter mess. You can just feel that the devs are struggling to find an identity for this game. They are very much pushing it to be competitive but they are also pulling it back to try and be casual and fun. It's just not working, In doing so they have created an unbalanced chaotic mess of a game. they need to pick one or the other and begin balancing gameplay around it, because if league has proved anything, it is that you can't make a game super competitive and expect people not to get frustrated with it. You either need to balance for competitiveness or casual fun, you just can't have both.

If you want a tl;dr I really recommend the game. If you're interested in reading the full thing I'll go into detail about what makes the game special and why it's one of the most fun games I've gotten into.

Omega Strikers is a fast paced 3v3 game that's easy to understand yet has a very high skill ceiling if you're willing to put in the effort. The game is getting balance changes through micropaches on a regular basis and is designed in a very competitive way that's designed for players that want a game to get good at and compete against others.
If you're not looking for a game to become good at but rather for a game to play with your friends I still recommend the game as it's easy to understand and get into as the principles aren't very complicated and due to it being free there's really no harm in giving it a go.

The base principal is two teams of 3 players trying to get a ball (the core) into the enemies goal. The game has different characters with different abilities that can be used to try to score or defend a goal. Instead of trying to get a goal there is also the option of killing enemy players in order to gain a player advantage while the enemy player is waiting for their respawn timer to expire. The default gamemode is a best of 5 game of singular sets that are also run in a best of 5 fashion.

Omega Strikers offers different characters that can all be played in both a goalie and a forward position. Although most characters seem like they're designed for a specific position all characters can be played in both roles and perform surprisingly well, too. A team always consists of a goalie and two forwards and while both roles essentially get similar tools and have access to the same characters there's a different depth to them.

A goalie has the job to defend the goal and stop the enemy team from scoring and while it seems like a simple task that means you're constantly fighting enemy forwards trying to score. The role of a goalie can become very complicated and include reads as your shot has a cooldown meaning if you shoot first the enemy can simply shoot past you, and while trying to get that right you also have to account for abilities that might get thrown at you.
When playing a forward you're on the other side, you're trying to get the core past the enemy forwards and the goalie. While there's still similar reads involved the role of a forward means you'll have to pressure the enemy goalie into making a mistake and try to find ways past them. A goalie's role can be very stressful due to mistakes being potentially game changing when the core enters your own goal.
Both roles are equally complex and have a high skill ceiling which results in most players having a preferred position to play in. 

The game manages to not feel the same every game by having different maps and awakenings.
The difference between maps consists of different kinds of hazards. Some maps use gravity fields to influence the way the core moves meaning you'll have to adapt your shots while also getting to go for angled strikes. Another map has a huge wall through the middle essentially splitting it up into two rows that you have to defend. In addition to that a goal has to be opened first by hitting a hazard in front of it. Some maps only have one of these triggers but others have two that both need to be activated for the goal to open.
And there's the awakening system. Awakenings are powerups buffing different skills of your character (e.g. ranged hits or projectiles, your health, your speed or your strength) that get drafted between sets. Players get to pick an awakening in an order based on how active they were in the set resulting in your exact build changing each game.

In my personal opinion the game has a lot of potential to grow as a competitive game and I'm looking forward to see where the game is headed for the future. With active updates and support from its developers it's a game that has everything it needs to stick around for a longer time and I hope to see it grow to become a more well known esports title.

One of the most fun games I've played in months, with a developer that isn't hellbent on milking you for every penny you have, but good luck trying to have fun in unranked gamemodes. There's no unranked MMR, meaning it's a coin toss of who gets the room temperature IQ team mates playing on their phones in the subway. Another coin toss then decides whether they play the game, rage quit, afk, or just keep passing the ball into the enemy instead of to their teammates. If you're extra lucky, you might even end up with Challenger (aka the highest rank) player on the enemy team. Good luck!

[h1] The unranked experience [/h1]
Look, I know what you want to say: "Sounds like a skill issue" or "It's not your teammates, it's you!" but let me tell you, because it's a 3v3, a single clueless player can quickly ruin the game, which shouldn't be a problem as the game is fundamentally not hard, yet you see so many people making seemingly basic mistakes that are impossible to fix mid-game. If you're playing goalie and your forwards aren't passing to each other, you can't just leave the goal arc and do your own thing. Similarly, if you're playing forward and your goalie keeps passing to the enemy or your other forward doesn't pass to you, you can't just chase the ball, as that'll leave one area of the map undefended; you also can't just help your goalie out since most of the time, it'll make things worse. I do feel like it's partly caused by the completely useless tutorial, which barely teaches you anything, so I can hardly blame the players (unless they insist on defending MY goal when I've spammed "let me defend" 10 times already this round. Seriously, GET OUT).

[h1] Communication, or rather the lack thereof [/h1]
But of course, some will simply say: "Just tell your teammates"
Well, friend, I would love to, but in their infinite wisdom, the devs decided that the absolute best way to combat toxicity is to not combat it at all and instead remove every traditional form of communication from matches. Want to plan strats with your team? Nope. Callouts? Nope. Better get used to the communication wheel (which doesn't even work 30% of the time) and pray that your teammates can read (Spoiler: Judging by how often goalies play forward and vice versa, that chance is low).

[h1] The kill meta [/h1]
My other gripe with the game lies in the effectiveness of killing enemies. Can't score goals because you keep shooting from the same angle and the goalie keeps miraculously blocking the ball? Just kill the enemy! 
While I do respect the mechanic, the way it's executed often leaves me frustrated and unwilling to play further, as there are basically only three ways of countering it: 
1) You evade BEFORE you get hit, using up one of your 3 energy bars. This works well for attacks that allow you to react to them (e.g. Vyce's/Luna's special), but often doesn't cut it when you're trying to predict attacks as it only lasts for a very short while. It also doesn't buffer the input when you're getting stunned, meaning you can -if you're unlucky- get hit multiple times even when you've pressed the button, unless you spam it. All of this might be manageable, but if all 3 bars are full, using it on an evade is basically a waste, as it'll drain all three bars, leaving you completely defenseless. A separate keybind that allows you to fire an evade instead of a core flip would be a god sent here.
2) You have an Atlas on your team and he manages to predict your untimely demise, buying you a few more seconds. Unfortunately, this means you're ♥♥♥♥ out of luck for the next 40 or so seconds, as that's his CD. This approach, as you might have guessed, often doesn't work, especially not if they decide to focus your Atlas instead.
3) Of course, you might think that simply walking away will save you, but in practice, it absolutely does not. The second you leave the exact middle of the map, any attack will knock you across the globe and out of the arena, putting you into the cameraman POV for the next 14 seconds. Sure, you can try your luck at one of the orb respawn locations, but they're conveniently placed at the edges of the map, meaning a well-placed attack can and will knock you out. Your only other option is not getting hit for about 15 seconds until your health has regenerated sufficiently. Maybe it's just me, but I think killing is just far too strong right now and the devs seem to be oblivious to it.

[h1] Microtransactions & The battlepass [/h1]
That said, there is something amazing to be said about the developers, as the battle pass is incredibly easy compared to some more recent titles. Yes, there are microtransactions, but the game is not grindy at all, you can quickly unlock whatever and whoever you want. A lot of the emotes are hilarious and give the game a more wholesome vibe. The game definitely respects your time when it comes to currencies, which is a breath of fresh air in modern video games, especially considering IT'S FREE. Unfortunately, I think that may also be part of the reason why the game, to put it bluntly, is dying. There's no reason to play (other than for fun, which is a good thing) once you've unlocked everything, there's no greedy battlepass forcing you to log in every day only to get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reskin after 4 weeks, there are no gacha pulls, no FOMO, nothing that gets the average Joe with his fried dopamine receptors and attention span of a goldfish playing continuously.

[h1] Social system? What social system? [/h1]
The social system is so horrendous it may as well be non-existent, as there is none of the common functionality present in other (and much older) titles. Indeed, truly revolutionary features such as DMs or party indicators (e.g. whether a friend if playing, queueing, in a party, etc.) do not exist in Omega Strikers, which doesn't help with player retention at all, more on that below.

[h1] Ranked matchmaking [/h1]
There have been complaints about smurfing, but I haven't encountered any while playing ranked (at an average level). Still, the matchmaking can be unpredictable, as you'll sometimes get matched with players 3-4 ranks above/below you. It doesn't matter if your goalie is diamond, your low silver forward will ♥♥♥♥ it up anyway (which isn't necessarily their fault).

With all that said, do I recommend it? Yeah, kind of. It's definitely fun when you're playing with friends or just messing around, but beware that if you play solo (especially unranked) as you might leave with permanent brain damage. Maybe I just had bad luck, but that doesn't make me feel any better. I'd also love to hear others' opinions on this, as I've had mixed responses talking about the aforementioned issues with friends.

The only real criticism I have is that the in-game prices for the characters are not uniform. Newer characters are significantly more expensive with in-game currency, and its not that cheap too unlock the whole roster.

You can unlock private matches with friends, however everyone has to have their own copy of the game and clear the tutorial. I little bit of a hassle if you want play with just friends. 

Otherwise, this is fun unique team action sport. I wish them enough success to smooth out some of these rough edges along the way.

Overall I think this game is really fun! But it's got a few big flaws that I think can really hurt someone's motivation to play it. So despite the fact that I enjoy the core game and can overlook these problems myself, I'm leaving a negative in hopes that these flaws can get patched up.

- Cannot permanently/globally mute emotes
This is the biggest issue I take with the game. Emotes in this game are mostly adorable- but also large with poppy sound queues. They're easily distracting and players should be able to opt out of seeing them at all if it gets in the way of them playing well.
Flaming through emotes is also pretty common, which can be a huge turnoff for new players to go into matches themselves. I have nothing against emotes that can function in this way, but it's just another reason not being able to mute them is, in my opinion, a huge flaw.
The individual mutes hardly work as a band-aid; and even if you individually mute a toxic player, your next game with that same player will have them unmuted. 

- Competitive/standard matches go for too long
Ranked so far has been prone to ragequitters, and leveling combined with the item selection set-up feels pretty snowball-y, further encouraging a losing team or a player that's particularly behind to just stop trying. Best of 3 seems like a better fit for the average player.

- Item selection feels bad.
I can understand the desire to give the winning players the edge, but I think everyone should have just a tiny bit more control over what kind of items they can get even if they're behind.

- It could take a few days to get your ideal character as a new player.
In my opinion, every hero based game should give you a pick one. Omega Strikers gives you a few bonuses as a new player, but it may still take you a few days to clutch that 50k currency character you want. 

- Tutorial is lacking
Beyond controls and a rough idea of what forward and goalie do, there are a number of unspoken rules that go with your role and characters that the game does not teach you. Additional tutorials that go over more advanced concepts would help new players that don't have mentors to show them the ropes.

Character balance seems decent- there aren't really any characters I feel like I can't handle fighting. Matchmaking starts out rough, but once you learn some basics closing the skill gap doesn't feel impossible. Monetization feels fair and completing the battle pass as a casual player isn't unreasonable. 

Beyond my complaints for it, this is probably the first competitive game I've genuinely enjoyed my time with. I rarely play any by myself and have been playing on my own pretty regularly since I started last week. I will continue playing and will look out for improvements to the game's systems.

Coming back to write more about this game, because, yes, it still has me sucked in. Omega Strikers is seriously unlike anything I've ever played. No other game can scratch the itch that this game does.

New players, I'll tell you right now: the first week or so of playing kinda sucks. It feels like you have no idea what you're doing while everything is moving so fast. I went through it when I first started playing. But then, you make your first goal, you make a good cooperative play with a teammate, you learn how to do something cool with your character. That's when the game gets good. The learning curve is steep, but once you get over it, it's seriously so much fun.

Let's go over pros and cons (cons first, because I'd like to end with pros).

CONS
-Small player base. If you're not playing on NA or JP servers, it's hard, or sometimes near impossible to find a game.
-Steep learning curve, as previously mentioned
-Toxic players, but every multiplayer game inevitably gets some
-Ranked matchmaking is... messy. With such a small player base, you'll often times get matched up with people that are not the same rank as you. Could be higher, could be lower, who knows.
-Odyssey is currently focusing on developing a new game, so OS gets pushed to the side a fair bit. But it has not been completely left behind, contrary to popular belief.

PROS
-Absolute banger soundtrack. Each character has their own theme song, and it plays when that character gets MVP. Genuinely one of my favorite parts of the game. Thousand Absolutes will never fail to hype me the hell up.
-No text chat. Only form of communication is through a large library of emotes (but you can only equip 7, so choose them wisely). Yes, there are toxic emotes and they can be used in irritating ways, but you can mute them! And more often than not, emote interactions are actually quite wholesome.
-Fairly active (as far as I know) competitive community; small, but mighty. Many people are willing to coach you if you ask! There's also a hefty creative community, if the competitive aspect isn't your thing.
-Cool characters with unique abilities, and each of them gets their own lore (some more than others, but lore nonetheless). 
-ITS FUN!! ITS GENUINELY FUN!! It's fast and exciting!
-It's free!!

I absolutely loved this game in beta. It was a breath of fresh air in the competitive gaming landscape, with a novel concept that was easy to pick up but difficult to master. My main criticism comes from a change to a core game mechanic (masteries → items) that is making the game more frustrating than fun.

My stance on mechanics in competitive games is that you have to strike a balance between consistency (more competitively balanced) and variability (less competitively balanced). If a mechanic is consistent, then player skill is the primary factor when it comes to victory. If a mechanic is variable, then randomness has a larger impact on outcomes. Something is bland if it's overly consistent, frustrating if it's overly random, and fun if it's reached a sweet spot where it is both.

Having different fields is fun: there are different maps with different goal barriers and hazards. It's variable in that its random, but consistent in that you play the same map the whole game. It's not consistent in the way that summoner's rift or the field in rocket league are always the same, but that adds charm and you know at character select so you can plan and adapt accordingly.

Having different strikers is fun: having a cast of characters with different abilities, specialties, and roles is fun. There's variability in terms of balance, but when you consider that the only 'balanced' competitive game is Street Fighter 1, having options makes for a fun experience.

The change from masteries to itemization went from one extreme (consistency) to another (randomness), and makes the game unnecessarily frustrating by stacking too many layers of randomness on top of each other and almost entirely sacrificing the consistency of a striker's play style.
- The two main starting items you can choose from are random
- The items you can choose from between sets are random (they even removed the one layer of consistency by having one item that is available to everyone)
- The order in which you can pick these items are random (at least I hope they are now, it felt like they used to be weighted so those who performed best got first dibs, which would lead to snowballing in what could have been a nice comeback mechanic).

When you take these last two points and multiply them across a minimum of two sets and a maximum of four sets, there is substantial variability in how well (or poorly) your striker functions after anywhere from three to nine layers of randomness in itemization. I'm not saying that the game needs to necessarily revert to masteries, but introducing *some* level of consistency would do some good in ensuring the long-term competitive viability of this game. This could be achieved in a number of ways: you could keep the items random but make them all infinite-choice (which could be further balanced by having fewer items available to pick from, or at least making each item available to two players before removing it from the choice pool). You could switch to currency/shop system (e.g., League) where all items are available and players can freely itemize to either maximize their own striker's strengths, cover their weaknesses, counter their opponents, or adapt to different roles (thus allowing characters with kits who can be used in different roles to more freely spec into those roles).

Change is fine and even good for a game's longevity, but for how large an aspect of the game it is, the current itemization system feels too random and as a result too frustrating. As a player, my immediate thoughts when I queue up are "will the game roll items that will let my character feel fun?" and "even if it does, will I even be able to get them?" When things line up, I feel on top of the world and able to play to my fullest, but when they don't I feel like I'm playing a gutted shell of a character for no reason other than that the layers of RNG weren't in my favor. Any changes to restore more degrees of player agency would be appreciated.

In that review, I said I could NOT recommend Omega Strikers in it's current state. A few technical reasons were cited (some of which have since been resolved) but the biggest reason I suspected this game would fall to the wayside was a lack of engagement for casual, PvP-adverse players.

Currently, and now possibly permanently, Omega Strikers only has ONE non-PvP mode for players to engage in, "Coop vs AI", which involves playing on the exact same basic stage against the exact same 3 bots at the same level of difficulty they always are... and if that doesn't sound annoyingly repetitive and disengaging enough for you, you STILL have to queue into matchmaking because, get this, you can't have AI teammates. You still need OTHER PLAYERS on your team, so even when you just want to relax and thrash some bots, not only do you not get to customize the game... AT ALL... you also have to WAIT for TWO OTHER YUTZES to somehow want to play the same boring game mode you're queuing up for and guess what your wait times on THAT can look like!?

This is not even the bare minimum of engagement for non-PvP players. This is somehow UNDER that bar via the complete lack of customization and the inability to solo queue with bot allies (even though there are bots on the enemy team so... it's not like bot allies are IMPOSSIBLE...)

And if you think "well gee, Darkest King... that's an awful lot of complaining about PvE stuff in a game that's definitely built to be PvP focused", you're right.

I'm a casual, PvE kind of guy. I like casual, PvE kind of experiences. But you know what?

I also play Smash Bros and StarCraft 2. These are games with MASSIVE competitive scenes but also TONS to offer non-PvP players and if you think those two things are unrelated then I think you're forgetting that so many PvP'ers started off like me, casual PvE'ers who fell so in love with the game that they got curious to try out the one thing left to do in that game after they've done everything else: compete.

Well, now... it doesn't look like Omega Strikers will be doing much competition anymore...

They did say they are going to potentially continue adjusting custom game modes so perhaps there is hope there, but unless it involves allowing players to set up custom games with bots (both enemy AND ally), play it solo, customize the map, rules, items, bot characters AND bot difficulty levels? Omega Strikers is as good as dust in the wind...
