Arena battles, tabletop hockey, MOBAs... these elements may seem incompatible, but Omega Strikers manages to combine them to create a unique gaming experience for players. Despite the abundance of creative games in recent years, Omega Strikers still has enough distinctive features to attract players.

With its colorful anime-style scenery and characters, intense and fast-paced battles, highly customizable and random gameplay, and fun game design, Omega Strikers is truly addictive and has great potential.

However, there are some issues with Omega Strikers at present. The 3v3 player design makes the game field seem crowded, and new players often have trouble seeing their character's location. The lack of practice modes and diverse game modes may make the game lose its freshness and fail to retain players in the long term. I think the balance of characters also needs improvement. As a cross-platform online game, the game's graphics have been somewhat compromised, and mobile players have an advantage in terms of simpler operations.

Overall, Omega Strikers is a game with great potential. However, it still has some issues, and the 3v3 team competition makes team coordination crucial. Playing with friends may be a better choice, especially since there is currently a lack of communication and interaction among teammates in the game. Therefore, if you are a lone wolf player, I do not recommend wasting time playing competitive games with strangers.

3) The game is EXCELLENT with a group of friends, but it's a mixed bag with randoms. Mileage may vary but this is a great free game you can pretty quickly get a group rolling with. Long term will decide if the progression and season pass systems in place are reasonable, but so far the out of the gate currency + Daily missions + Daily log ins do give me the inclination that I can probably grind out most of the cast fairly quickly, and I've found the starting characters can absolutely hold their own with no problems.

[b]TL;DR[/b] I have been having a lot of fun playing the game. Despite matches ("normal" and "competitive" modes) becoming longer in terms of length/time they appear a lot more varied and force some thought/adaptation, which I think is cool. And you can get some cool cosmetic stuff just by playing the game (not skins, but still very epic, in my opinion). Other than a tutorial, they have added a CO-OP VS. AI mode to the game to practise in a safe environment, but there isn't any real "shooting range" or a way to repeat a tutorial in case you went through one beforehand. Other than that, I think it is very fun and a worth a shot.

The rest of this is just my personal in-depth look of some the changes that they have added now after the beta. Apologies for the length.

[h1] Small disclaimer [/h1]
[strike]I don't know if I can call this a review, since I am mostly glaring over the new changes that the developers have added. And for the most part the type of changes that I like (other people may not and I think that is fair).[/strike] I added in a part talking about match structure as well as a tl;dr. That is about it.

[h1] Gameplay-related [/h1]

The game is very fun. When comparing to the beta that happened in 2022, I think some of the new changes are something that can take a bit of time to get used to, but overall I do think they add more depth to the overall game. Even though I think it became slightly more methodical and the matches became a bit longer as a result, I definitely think some of the new changes are very cool.

For example, I think the addition of the evade/burst button functions both as a good counter against players who are playing offensively (by that, I mean attempt to knock you off the arena) as well as a sort of a an equivalent of a reverse UNO card. By the latter I mean that you can use it to stop the core (the equivalent of a hockey puck in this game), knock all enemies back AND be the only one to deal a powerful attack on the core (for the time it is in the air), which can cause it to zip through the field very fast. It is also quite risky to use, as the moment you strike the core (or don't attack it on time, like I did a few times), enemies can easily hit it back/ continue hitting it as normal. It can serve as a good way to break up the usual back and forth hits from one side to another and even be used to dunk a surprise goal on the enemy team (if you time it right).
In order to use this ability the player must fill up an energy bar (indicated under the player's health or stagger bar). In order to use the ability to evade, you only need to fill up a quarter of the bar, while the burst option requires you to fill up the entire bar of energy.
I personally think it is a great and simple addition, as it provides both safe and risky options of use and implemented in a way that makes it improbable to abuse.

I also think the way they handled maps in the new "normal" mode is cool. There are not as many, but they have some cool gimmicks to them (like speed pads, an orbital field in the middle of the map which changes the direction of a struck core and some other stuff). They also made them less intense when playing  as goalies. Before anyone can score a point, you first have to knock down 2 barriers (by hitting them once), which will open up the gates. This allows more room for mistakes on the goalie's side (or just the team's side), but not too many to make it lack intensity. And even with barriers down a good goalie and/or team can handle the pressure.

[h1] Match sturcture, gears and awakenings [/h1]
I think the changes to the match structure (dividing them into sets and adding upgrades in-between sets) are interesting in a good way. I can't really talk about these without mentioning the "Trainings" system that the game had beforehand.
 Previously the game had a system called "Trainings". They are basically small and simple loadouts consisting of 3 cards that could adjust specific characteristics of each character you chose to play (some could adjust projectile speed or increase their size, others could increase your character's hitbox and the strength of your attacks and etc.). The idea behind them was cool in my opinion, however, there were small drawbacks to them. Each one was basically divided into a category (stuff related to damage, speed, cooldowns, size changes for characters or the things they could make appear, were all separate). And each character would have 2 pre-determined categories of slots they could use and one slot which could use a training from any of the given categories.  These often had around 5 trainings to pick from. This would not be a real problem if  only one or two were to appear to be suitable for a specific character. And sometimes only one specific training would appear to be the most appealing for a variety of different characters. This could result in customization being limited and "samey". On top of that, you could encounter different people using the same meta-driven builds with the same characters and it would make these encounters slightly more boring.

This brings me to the currently existing version of the game. "Trainings" were transformed into "Gears" and "Awakenings". They are basically the adjusted / reworked versions of the original "Trainings", where "Awakenings" are distributed at the start and in-between match sets, while "Gears" are given out only at the start of each match.

"Gears" are always the same and they do not change. You can only pick one per match.

"Awakenings" always change. Starting from the beginning of the round you will have a choice between two random awakenings. In-between sets you will have a choice between 8 different "Awakenings", but as soon as someone chooses a specific one, that one will no longer be available for others to pick. The pick order for these is determined by how well you have played the previous round. This can mean that you may or may not get the opportunity to get a chance to get a specific "Awakening".
Although it has RNG-based elements, there are still ways to tip the coin to your favor and it forces you from the very beginning to think about which character to pick and how to play. It is also a good opportunity to prevent your opponent from picking an "Awakening" that could immnesely benefit them.  And even if you enjoy playing a specific character, pretty much all the time there will be an "Awakening" which will benefit you one way or another. It just forces constant adaptation and I think that is a good thing and makes even a single match quite varied. Besides that on their own, they won't actually determine how skilled or well-knowledged you are. 

Their inclusion though, does however, end up impacting match length, which is one of the main drawbacks. 
It did not diminish my personal enjoyment of the game.

[h2] Small conclusion on this part [/h2]

Overall, I think the inclusion of these changes makes the game slightly slower-paced and methodical in some regards, but also adds the necessary amounts of depth to make the overall experience a lot more varied and still remain as fun to play.

[h1] Some other stuff I liked at the moment [/h1]
I like the new affinity related stuff they made for each character. It basically allows you to unlock  small cosmetic stuff and in-game currencies for the character you like playing the most (and with the affinity tokens you can get from missions you can also try other characters). That is one of the few reasons I did not really play this game as often.

[h1] A small endnote [/h1]
I'd offer to actually try and play the game. The developers seem friendly and the overall atmosphere of the game (aside from intense matches) is pretty chill. I personally ain't good at it, but I find it very fun.

I suppose I get to come in here and throw in yet another complaint about the new changes to the game and hope the devs can understand the feelings of the community. The beta was a near-perfect game. At the core, the game still is fun, the issue is that it has now been almost entirely scrapped for a game that is different enough to be almost a bad copy of the beta version. We got hit with a real life mobile game ad. It's an almost textbook case of developers not knowing when to stop because they feel like they can continue to improve, when they already have one of the most enjoyable games I've ever gotten to play. Ok so here we go.
This game slaps, probably a 9/10 in pure mechanics if we're being honest. it knows what it is and it does aspects of that very well. I'm gonna list out so pros and cons below.

Pros:
good control scheme.
good controller and keyboard support with multiple variations of keyboard.
very low latency, no rubberbanding.
fun classes.
simplistic but high skill ceiling gameplay.
just a good time especially with friends.

Cons:
paywall classes
class balance
limited replayability

So as you can see above the pros are strong but the Cons are actually quite a big deal and they impact this game more than you might think. each match in this game last about 3-7 minutes and replayability is a huge factor. you can pretty easily knock out 10 matches in an hour if the Queue times are low.
the area this starts to become an issue with is class balance and the pay wall.
they are fairly generous with initial currency but unlocking 3+ classes will require about 20 hours and it slows from there.
this causes an issue where balance is concerned. certain characters are just better than others overall. since your characters can "die" and the game is simple enough in core concept a "bruiser character who can bully other people actually damages the concept a bit. if they walk up and kill a character in a few seconds it suddenly becomes a 3v2 for about 10 seconds and if they start bullying another character while the third is dead it basically becomes a 3v1.

the worst part about this is it feels bad, and not in the just getting outplayed way, but when you can't avoid the other character because its impossible and you can't fight back because they are stronger and then they kill you and score a goal by pushing you both into the goal area it feels broken.

outside of this the actual gameplay is fun. the team work is lovely and playing with friends is a blast but if you play against a team with even a single player who is combat focused and playing X it just ruins the game basically. you can have people on both teams play X I guess but then you have the issue of being forced to have a single person in every single game or being put at a disadvantage.
it's really a shame. I think removing the ability to kill players or changing how the combat works would go a long way into saving this game.

While it may seem like I do not have a lot of time in-game, this community has genuinely been one of the nicest communities I have been in. I never thought the removal of chat in a game could affect the community so much but I am so happy to have been proven wrong. I hope that whatever odyssey cooks up for the omegaverse does OS justice. [h3] Anyways... [/h3]

 [h2] I don't think text alone can describe how I feel about this game. [/h2]

When I first saw the game in beta, I instantly liked it, but sadly my phone was very weak for the mobile beta, and I didn't have a laptop to play the beta. But I knew the game would be good from the clips I was seeing.

I wanted to play on release, but I couldn't play much due to irl things, yet I still enjoyed the game. From then on when I could play, I knew the game was for me and I played a LOT of it, and even entered some tournaments.

 I played it for a very long while, getting about 100 hours in 2-3 weeks. I burnt out a bit so I stopped playing and came back around at the end of S2.

Then S2 hit, and at the start I wanted to play a lot, but I really couldn't find myself due to how bad soloq comp was, but I did because of the community. This community has been genuinely nice to me both in general and helping me get better (also for giving me funny moments to post on @/sussystrike), and I couldn't ask for any different one.

This game means a lot to me. It's one of the 2 games that is genuinely the reason I started playing games competitively again (and was one of the games I was somewhat good at 🙏). I don't think I could've asked for any other game like this one, especially with how unique it is... and I know that no matter what multiplayer game I play, it won't have an impact like OS did.

This game was one of the few games my and my partner both sucked at, yet enjoyed every second we spent on it. Although we didn't play much, we loved it.

To everyone at Odyssey, bravo on the amazing game... I hope everything in the future goes perfectly for you guys, you all deserve the best for genuinely listening to your players (I made the custom game feedback and they listened :D) and not making the game P2W in anyway.. 🙏💙

To everyone I met on the journey, thank you for all the memories, funny times, and general amazing vibes you all have given. Hoping to make more even beyond today. 🫡

And to everyone who doesn't know me just now reading this, but did play OS... I hope you enjoyed the game. 😊

An incredibly fun take on the classic air hockey type games. There's a lot of potential here for a really stellar game and I can only hop it's capitalized on in the future. 

The creativity to keep each round fresh is pretty impressive as well. Burst, artifact drafting, and goal buffers all make each match feel much more fair and skill based rather than how it used to be, where every character would assault the core as much as possible and some abilities would simply have better priority. 

Aside from the gameplay, the soundtrack is ok, but I wouldn't listen to it in my free time. It certainly has a high energy feel but it can get a bit repetetive. Perhaps eventually there will be a larger selection or a sort of jukebox with unlockable lobby music? Only a thought but some variety would be nice.

And finally the art direction. Overall the game is very bright and cel-shaded, but not so much that it hurts (most of the time). It can get a bit confusing with so many abilities happening at once but it's usually tolerable. Now for UI design. The HUD in an actual match is pretty good, clean and doesn't take up space. Some customization for placement would be nice, however. It can be annoying to try and keep track of your cooldowns when it's in the corner of the screen, but that might just be me. Perhaps small icons on the mouse as an option? I don't know, I don't design games. Moving on to the UI for the menus, I they feel just a little lacking. Not by a lot, but I feel like the shop menus are just a bit bulky. Same for the quests menu.

Overall I have high expectations and hope that the game is only improved with time! :D

Edit: I come back having taken some time away from the game to cooldown to write something more proper for a game I was quite excited for when it initially released. While my opinion certainly hasn't changed I do want to expand on that initial gut reaction to the changes. 

The maps have gotten significantly more annoying with deadzones in the middle, as well as added goal shields that just keep rounds dragging on and are harder to hit than your actual goal. Overall though I'd say that aspect of the changes are the most up to personal preferences- if you were into the smash aspect of the game you'll probably dig them. 

As for the loadout changes, they remove a large aspect of the strategy of the game in favour for long winding half hour to hour long games where the winner is often clear by the end of the second set. The players take turns drafting from a set of items to enhance their abilities, with the higher performing players drafting first. This leads to the already better performing players that game snowballing advantage especially if the first set of items offered is among the generically best or particularly good for their chosen character. 

Because of course, the offered items are completely random which is as unnecessary as it is pointlessly complex. Ideally in my mind they would simply add back the old system or, if that was to broken or easy to game, make needed changes to each characters basekit and just gut the items entirely.

Essentially every change in the Closed Beta absurdly lowers the game's quality. Matches are slower, to the point that there is almost no intensiveness anymore. New build systems are simultaneously  RNG, snowbally, and, oncemore, slow the game down extremely. To be fair, I believe the rewards system to be better than previous. Yet everything mechanically / within the games are devoid of what I played the game for to begin with. Without stating any of the mechanics themselves, all I can state is that I wish for plenty of reverts back to how the game was in the open alpha.

Overall with many many... maybe even too many hours at the moment of Omega Strikers, I can easily say this game is by far one of the better games in development that I've play tested in the past 5 or 6 years. I've been playing this game since February of 2022 in it's Alpha iteration. Like most games, there are obvious positives or negatives but the general experience I've had with the game was nothing more than overwhelmingly positive.

The major pros of the game are as following:
[list]
    [*]Fast action game-play allowing for great replay-ability and an overall less tilting experience game by game.
    [*]Interesting dynamic between a 3v3 brawler and air hockey game, allowing for lots of variety and ways to play the game to set win conditions.
    [*]Amazing design. From characters, to soundtracks, to level design everything feels very well thought allowing for a very lively and hype atmosphere. Absolutely love the personalities of the entire cast of characters, their interactions and their stories.
    [*]A wonderful developer team. Very highly responsive and constantly showing large amounts of care towards their product and community. The developers actively engage with the community and read feedback to better improve the quality of the game and experience it provides. I have never seen such a caring team as this one before in games I've played especially competitively.
    [*]An awesome community. Hands down this game has one of the most amazing and wholesome communities out there behind it, definitely easy to say that I'm more than happy to have found it and became apart of their community both online and on their official discord server. Made a lot of wonderful friends here and I'm excited to meet many more individuals as the game continues past release later this year.
[/list] 

That being said, not every game is perfect and has flaws, especially while in Beta. Most of which are most notably being already worked on and addressed in hopes of a highly successful launch.

The major negatives of the game as of Beta Test in my opinion are:
[list]
    [*]Not enough depth. Currently in Omega Strikers while games are very replay-able and fun, at a more competitive level especially the game lacks depth and requires more to it to make the game feel even more skillful. Currently there is some skill involved in regarding timing and ability usage, however there needs to be more elements added to really enhance the overall experience within it's game-play. This thankfully seems to be addressed in a much recent update announcement post and I can't wait to see how these changes take place on the game's full release.
    [*]A lack of social features. Currently all there really is in the game is a friend's list where you can add and invite players to your group/party. There's no real way to communicate with players outside and inside of matches aside from very vague quick actions during a match. Another very key issue is the limit of the friends list only being set at '100', this really needs to get increased for release as it's just way too low especially for streamers like myself. These issues also seems to be addressed in the recent update announcement post which is fantastic.
    [*]The Ranked & Elo system. Currently there are a handful of issues with this system most likely due to a low player count. However, that being said the matchmaking system struggles to really effectively put players within the same skill level and rank into the same match, especially during the second half of the Beta. This can cause for tons of frustration towards both the higher and lower rated players and can easily cause the experience to deter them from playing more. Another key issue is how the currently leader board and highest rank "Omega" works within the game. Due to the rank being achieved and never decayed or being a top % based rank a lot of top players have chose to sit on their accounts and make new alt accounts instead as they have less incentive to keep playing at that top level, which has caused a smurfing problem which has been slightly influential within the game less noticeably at lower elos but around mid - high elos. My hopes are that when the game fully releases, the player base can continue to grow to prevent these issues, but I do think some sort of system should be placed around the rank "Omega" to provide those players more incentive to keep playing on their accounts without feeling any need of having to create new accounts to continue playing in Ranked.
[/list]

I gave this game a positive review in beta, and was iffy on it post release, but it definitely needs to change now.

They keep making it more and more arcadey, and it really makes this a feels bad game. The game doesn't allow you to get a feel for anything because the variables of a game are always different. This was intentional from the devs, since they felt like the short matches back in beta all felt too similar, and would lead to players getting bored. But they have gone so far in the other direction that there is no real baseline for you too get used to. Kind of like playing a MOBA but you select items and ability upgrades at random. The maps used to be simple fields, but now they are all crazy ♥♥♥♥ and shapes flying everywhere that make it almost impossible to make precise plays. The game feels incredibly sloppy to play nowadays, since your character isn't consistent in how they play and the maps are often awkwardly shaped. Technically, this leads to a potentially enormously high skill ceiling if you CAN be incredibly precise, keeping all these variables in mind, but in practice it seems to lead to the problem that the population of the game faces right now. The games is mostly (note: not exclusively) populated by either people who are able to be very good at it, or people who are very bad at it. People in the middle, or newbies who manage to start to get good at the game, are few and far between, leaving due to frustration. This has created a self sustaining loop. Fewer people of a middling skill level means that more solo/duo queuers get stuck with new or bad players, who cause frustration since this is a VERY team centric game. These players then leave, ensuring less mid level players. There is a really simple reason for the changes from a competitive game with consistent play throughout the whole match, with only base stats like speed, hp, and power increasing as the game went on, to a wacky arcade style mobile game. I really wish they would add it back, even as an alternate game mode, for players who want that kind of experience.
If they stay on their current course, I can only imagine this game will become a game of a few high level hardened veterans and a few new players who trickle in and out. This is essentially death for a game, which is a real shame since this game was really something special. If they want to abandon this side of their player base entirely, just take it off steam, I could at least forget about the good old days.

Omega Strikers is great idea in theory. In practice, it's just a worse version of Videoball.

There are several analog variables, interactions, status effects, and even character customization (to an extent). Much of this complexity adds more clutter than depth. Worse, the feedback design is subpar and I couldn't figure out what was going on in a match or how I was supposed to play. Finally, there is no training mode to even see what the mechanics do.

Action is a fairly simple thing in games, but Omega Strikers fails to present something clean and understandable. If the developers want to make this game great, here are my basic recommendations:

1. Characters should act as non-overlapping solid bodies. They should not be able to pass through each other (or the ball).
2. Hitstun / hitpause would do wonders for the clarity of interactions. Hitstun is an essential part of feedback design but seems to be completely missing in Omega Strikers.
3. There should be no customization (outside cosmetics). It distracts from the actual gameplay. Just make the characters unique and balance them.
4. Outside super moves, mechanics should not be balanced by abstract cooldown timers. They should be balanced around organic properties (space, time, power) the way fighting game moves are.
5. There must be a training mode. This is not negotiable. There are already great free-to-play competitive games like Fantasy Strike and Prismata that give the player all the tools they need to learn every nuance of gameplay and become a master. Omega Strikers should follow suit.

So here's a little touch-up on the game now that I've played it for longer and now that it's fully released.

Some opening remarks:
1. This game is still very new, if you are unhappy with how it is now, things are bound to change and new things will be added in the future. There is no right to be angry when there's still so much that can happen.
2. As someone who played during the beta, april fools playtest, and on release as a current mid-plat player, my opinion is strong but not as strong as others who played during the Alpha stages of the game, nor is my opinion as strong as the current/reoccurring top-ranks.

With that out of the way, let's begin.

I HIGHLY recommend this game to people, and I will reiterate this later on. Omega Strikers is genuinely one of the greatest games I have come around to play, originally hearing about it via word of mouth by one of my friends at school. I played during the open beta, which was originally a "First to Five, Win By Two" format. Really fun choice, but that has been phased out on release to a Best OF 5 format, this choice was smart, makes it feel more redeeming coming out of each post-set draft with a stronger gameplan and stronger awakenings.

Oh right, the draft system!
The draft system is very interesting, taking the MVP of whichever team won the set and allowing them to pick first, then scaled off of who did the best from then on. It's unique, allowing for a 'play better win more' mentality during each match.

The gameplay is fluid, the characters are well designed and their voice actors hit it out of the park!
The music for each of the characters are incredible, my personal favorite at the moment being Vice Versa, for the character called Vyce(Linked here https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Irp7G1N3Gkw). James Landino and the rest of the music guys are incredible at what they do, they deserve a huge round of applause for going insane with the soundtrack.

One last thing I want to mention; the community.
Omega Strikers has to have one of the greatest communities that I have seen in gaming, they're supportive, kind, and the devs that pop into chat whenever they can are always kind. It's rare that you see devs as kind as these, so that's a few extra points there.

Overall, this game is amazing, I highly, HIGHLY recommend this game for those who are looking for a great team-based experience. My personal advice to you, as a newcomer, is to enjoy the game and find people you have synergy with. To get your bearings, first play CO-OP Vs. AI to understand the mechanics. You will constantly learn new tech, positioning, passing plays, etc. as you go on about playing this game. I, myself, have found new tech that I haven't even thought about implementing into my games.

Biggest issue currently is the severely diminished active player community. One of the major drawbacks of this game is other players.

That, or they're "playing" doesn't count towards quests - it really brings down a game when you're goalie just refuses to do their job.

I would also like to see a training or AI mode implemented so players can feel more comfortable testing new characters and strategies. An offline mode would also help solve the problem of wait times and lack of players, especially for those of us using smaller servers (like Oceania).

Overall, really great game, but is a bit tedious waiting for games if/when you don't have friends to play with.

One of the most innovative games of the year. Omega Strikers is one of those games which rely mostly on player skill and not grinding nor getting OP equipment. Here you can play for free and unlock any character for ingame points you get from playing it. The premium part is character skins and extra emotes, the game doesn't force you to pay for anything required to get a decent character and unlock the best builds for them.

As for the difficulty curve. You can get frustrated in the first several matches as you don't know what to do and follow the core (name for the puck) mindlessly instead of positioning your Striker for it. The plethora of different characters and abilities also makes it super confusing as to what's going on. Once you get a hang of it, the game becomes clear and all the stuff that felt OP and impossible to evade becomes easy to counter. This goes especially for being knocked out, where new players don't realize that they're being KOed because they're too close to the edge and not because of their enemies being more powerful.

The graphics are simplistic but pretty. The overall character design is staggering when it comes for detail. Each Striker has their story and amazing voice acting. Some of the characters are hilarious, like the alien blob girl who wants to become human or the giant hamster Dubu. 

Gameplay itself is extremely well designed and very fast paced. The dynamics make it seem very unbalanced when it comes for playing with random players which might cause a lot of frustrations when you're playing against a very good team and your team mates struggle. It's especially annoying when a player who's designated as a goalie doesn't stay at the goal to protect it. This feels like a rather common thing in unranked mode where people are unfit to play goalie but choose the position regardless to complete a daily, expecting someone else on the team to get frustrated enough to cover the goalie spot instead of them. This is of course a non-issue for premade teams, so if you're playing with friends you don't need to care about those kinds of players turning up in your team.

As you progress you get more emotes, character skins etc. You also get certain rewards for completing certain tasks like reaching gold rank in ranked mode, for example, where you get an alternative skin that's only available for achieving that, and can't be bought. 

I highly recommend this game.

Odyssey announced yesterday that the game will not receive more than minor, non-content patches up until the end of the open beta period. While this is purportedly done to improve the gameplay for the full launch in order to increase player retention rates, it is a complete and utter neglect of the people who are currently playing and have supported Omega Strikers thus far. What is left for these people to look forward to? Absolutely nothing.

The issue is exacerbated by what appears to be Odyssey's ad hoc management of the game. With the previous patch in October, Odyssey had already announced that there was going to be less content up until the launch of the game, but at least two new strikers were promised. Then, yesterday, on the day that the first striker is supposed to launch, Odyssey renegs on that promise. The silhouette of the striker had been visible in the game for a month. Current players had been looking forward to it for a month. But then the rug is pulled out from under them at the very last second. This makes it seem as if delivering on your own promises and living up to the expectations of the current playerbase is of no importance to Odyssey.

I therefore have to give Omega Strikers a negative review despite loving the gameplay. I hope Odyssey's management of the game improves in the future.

Omega Strikers is a free, high-skill pvp game vaguely resembling air hockey if it was raised by a moba and only took the good parts of its upbringing. Fast paced, great characters and simple gameplay that allows for a lot of skill in almost every aspect. It's great in many ways, but also held back by a few issues

As it is free, I will start by addressing the issues many people have with free games, and then give a few tips on how to actually enjoy it
So first- Monetization. Everyone thinks of it when they see a free game. And I'm happy to report that it is good. There is a battlepass and some cosmetics, but everything related to game mechanics is available through a very reasonable price of ingame currency gained through playing. It is probably one of the best ways I've seen it done

Second, trolls and cheaters. I've actually not seen any cheaters, and only two people trolling in about 72 hours of play. Worries about this are accurate however, as the report function is somewhat poor and difficult to use. But also because anyone can hide their name. The name which you need to report them. So far I haven't seen anyone abuse this yet, but if they did, there would be no way to report them

Third, is it dying?
I sure hope not! But if it is, there are three things I would point out as being the probably cause of it losing players, or players just not staying with it after they try. So you can avoid these problems or at least mitigate the worst parts

First problem, moba controls as default. Your default control scheme (with mouse+keyboard) makes it impossible to play comfortably. Moba controls has you use your mouse to move your character, and you need your mouse to aim your abilities or shots. This means your mouse needs to be in two different places at once as you need to do things while you move. I'm not opposed to extra available control schemes. But as default? That is just madness. Giving first time players what amounts to a nonfunctional control scheme isn't going to encourage them to stay with the game and just puts more stress on them as they may not realize it is the control scheme that is working against them

Second, a lack of training mode and minimal tutorial. The tutorial only provides you the most basic lessons, and there is no training mode to try things out. Unlocked a new striker? Only way to try them and their abilities is in a game with other players. Have an idea for a new training loadout? Only way to try is by going into a game with other people who are unaware that you're experimenting. A single player testing zone, or a training thing against basic AI would help a lot. Throwing people in the deep end and telling them to just learn on the go doesn't work for everyone

And third, skill differences. As it is a game with a lot of skill involved and different sorts of skill matchmaking will be difficult. Often a match will be skewed in someone's favour, or you get matched with teammates who are worse than you by a large margin (Or better than you by a lot). This can lead to frustration when things are imbalanced too often and you get destroyed or teamed up with someone who isn't carrying their own weight. Or when you run into someone better on the other team who has a tactic that you don't know how to defend against

Either way I have not had very long queues even when playing at 10 in the morning on a workday. So for now the population still seems to be good enough for the game to function both on ranked and unranked

[b]Omega Strikers is a 3v3 competitive "soccer-ish sports game" with platform style combat and a simple set of rules with an insanely high skill ceiling. [/b]The first to 5 goals wins. However, the winner must be 2 points ahead. One player as a defender (goalie) and the other two players as the Attackers. This game has Esports written all over it. Developed by ex-Riot game developers, [u]Odyssey Interactive[/u], Omega Strikers is their debut game. Even in Open Beta, this game is very polished. 

Omega Strikers has this retro anime feel to it, with excellent sound effects (reminiscent of well crafted Nintendo sound effects), catchy and engaging music, and a UI that feels like a beautiful splash in the face of vibrant colors. Everything is so rich and colorful and welcoming. 

I have never been a fan of MOBAs or "Twitch eSports" types of game, but their is something so inviting about Omega Strikers. At the time of this review, I am roughly 4 hours in and I'm just now getting the hang of the gameplay. I personally have been struggling with controlling the direction I hit the core "puck" in with my mouse cursor while also controlling my characters movements. Placement on the field is everything.

There is an extensive cast of crazy looking characters, each with their own lore and sets of abilities. Some characters fair better at being the Defender while others are quicker, more agile, and fair better out on the field. But, you are free to select whoever you want for whichever role. 

Something must be said about how friendly Odyssey has made their monetization. It's almost all for cosmetics. I feel no need to spend money to "stay competitive" in this game. If I do end up dropping some dollars, it's because I want to support this passion project. 

This is the beginning of a new beautifully, well crafted competitive eSports game and I'm here for it.

I'm changing my negative review to a casual recommendation. However, I want to preface: Omega Strikers is not yet competitively viable. If you are expecting a compelling nuanced competitive experience like the branding suggests, prepare to be disappointed, or worse, frustrated. 

As a casual experience Omega Strikers is stellar. It reminds me of when I used to play Melee on my old CRT I got for $10 at a garage sale. Intuitive controls combined with open ended gameplay are the keystones to making an engaging and fulfilling skill curve that any player can progress at their own pace. If all you want is a fun, fast paced, team focused, hero hockey brawler, then why are you still reading this? Play the game already.

Since release, Odyssey has decided to move from rigid player customised Trainings to dynamic and unpredictable Awakenings. Both systems have pros and cons but I want to explain why Awakenings are healthier for both the competitive and casual ecosystems. Trainings allowed players to customise every Striker to their liking by specialising certain aspects of their kit. On paper this sounds great, players get to dictate their playstyle, refine consistent mechanics, and set their own win conditions. Unfortunately, it doesn't matter if your game has 12 or 12 billion loadout combinations, players will optimise them to find the best one. I still remember my first competitive game of Paladins. I got harassed and mass reported by my team because I was supposedly throwing for not having the exact specific meta loadout on my champion. In the end, loadout-esque player customisation does nothing but add a nuance filter to change the number of viable playstyles from 5 to 7. The second problem with Trainings is that every match only had two instances of counter play, when your team's second player chose their striker, and when your third player chose their striker. Striker selection was essentially like playing rock paper scissors, which is understandably how every hero based game works. However, most hero based games aren't played on a two dimensional one screen plane with nothing but periodically spawning green balls. There was no in game counter play, if you had scissors and they had rock, you were done.

Awakenings solve both of these issues while giving up a modicum of player agency by forcing you to adapt to the situation at hand not just strategically but mechanically as well. Each match starts with a random assortment of Awakenings, these are buffs applied to all players equally. This immediately removes a standardised meta as each striker's viability changes based on the randomly assorted Awakenings. Additionally, after each set (best of 5 goals), players enter a TFT style roulette to take their own Awakenings. This fixes the much needed counter play opportunity the game lacked before. If you picked scissors and they picked rock, you now have an opportunity to assess every angle of the situation; who has what, what your team needs, what you don't want their team to have, and calculate a new win condition accordingly. More importantly, this is astronomically better for casual players as it shakes up the monotony of each match.

So why don't I consider Omega Strikers competitively viable? The main reason is that a game of this calibre cannot have a balanced netcode, period. Due to the timing precision and pace, it is impossible for two players on opposite sides of the world to play chicken mind games on a balanced playing field. Even if you know what position your opponent is going to play, a slight unpredictable variation in ping is enough to turn your winning response into a losing one. It's essentially like rolling a dice to see who gets the last hit.

Finally, there are a number of quality of life, accessibility, and monetisation issues that I believe keep Omega Strikers from reaching the competitively viable experience it's branded as:
[list]
[*]Practice mode. Ideally with features like puck reset conditions (speed, angle), as well as managing barrier and redirect objects to simulate other players.
[*]Test out Strikers in the Store. This should be implemented along side practice mode.
[*]Cursor customisation. Essential feature, benign that its not here.
[*]Text chat.
[/list]

And some additional changes that I think would improve the user experience:
[list]
[*]Premium currency refund from BP.
[*]More emote binds.
[*]Option to disable emotes.
[/list]

What happens when you combine all the great aspects of League of Legends & Air Hockey? You get this masterpiece: an easy to pick up game with a roster of magnificently unique and complex characters that when combined with the fast paced 5-10 minute matches creates a high skill ceiling that leaves both casual and competitive players begging for more. Omega Strikers is still in its infancy; nonetheless, the Odyssey team has created something that is both a blast to play and lively to watch so not only can I recommend this game to anyone, I see great potential for Omega Strikers to be a mainstay in the ever-growing eSports scene.

All in all, a pretty solid hero-based soccer game. There are some things I'd change, and some characters will get balanced over time, but it's already pretty good. It's free to play, give it a try.

Positives:
The characters are all pretty stylish and unique (from each other, at least; it's a very anime-inspired style, though, so there are a lot of common tropes in the cast). And, they each feel pretty different to play, in a very good way. Even with only a couple hours of play, I can tell that there are a lot of ways that you can build skills for this game, and a lot of characters have a ton of potential to capitalize on high-skill play, but it's simple enough that it's not at all hard to get into (unlike something like Rocket League). 

It's very easy to boot up, find a game, and play for just a bit, no need to commit an hour or more of your time if you don't want to. The game runs very well, is very responsive, and doesn't waste your time with pre- or post-match timers. If you want to go from game to game, it's very snappy, and I appreciate the hell out of that.

Negatives:
The UI leaves a lot to be desired; they try to keep it minimalist and sleek, but the way it ends up is that there are a ton of important menus hidden in every corner of the screen, behind other menus, and you really have to hunt down how to do some stuff in the menus (it took me like 15 minutes to figure out how to make loadouts for my characters, and even after finding it, the menu itself is a PAIN to use) (also, you literally can't see how much currency you have while in the store menu, you have to back out to the top menu to see that). The controls in-game are much better, but I feel like they're not quite hitting their peak potential, with M+K or controller (I want a controller layout where I can aim my shots with the right stick while moving with the left, dangit! I so often hit it in the wrong direction while using controller, and managing the exact position of my cursor with M+K is tedious at best, but at least I can aim!). 

Some of the game feels weird, from the outset. You have a cooldown on your main kick button, so if someone hits the ball immediately after you do, your hit is completely cancelled out and the ball slips right past you; especially as a goalie, this feels like a very odd way to play. The maps are so small that the only real way to play is to rush the goalie, and try to hit the ball right after they do and slip it right under their legs. Also due to the small size of the arenas, you often end up with 3-4 players in the same spot, and keeping track of what the hell is happening when everyone's throwing around abilities is very difficult.

In terms of monetization, it's a free-to-play game, so of course it relies on microtransactions to stay afloat. However, currently, at launch, there are scant few options for things to buy; some characters don't even have a second skin, and the rest is stickers/emotes, and that's about it. I'm kind of worried that the game needs more -enticing- monetization options to make players want to support it. The tutorial missions give you a good amount of freemium currency, enough to buy a couple characters that interest you, aside from the starting four, but after that, it seems like earning currency might slow down a LOT, and getting more characters might take a long time (unless you pay real cash, of course).

The game also has a battle pass, because that's the new poison plaguing the industry, so be aware of that.

Overall:
Like I said at the top, it's a solid little game, give it a try because why not? Most of the gripes and issues I have with it can be fixed over time, if the devs keep working on it. With how short the matches are, and how flooded the market it wants to be in already is, I wish the developer a lot of luck in keeping it afloat. Give them just a bit of your time, try it out, consider buying a skin or 2 if you like it.
